2. Simple linear regression

MATH 4210, Chapter 2

Español

The Toluca Company builds refrigeration equipment and the replacement parts that keep it running. One part had long been produced in batches, or lots, of whatever size seemed convenient at the time. When the company started a cost-cutting review, its engineers wanted to settle a basic question: what lot size is cheapest to produce? Every production run carries a fixed setup cost that does not care about lot size, plus machining and assembly work that grows with the number of parts. To find the sweet spot, the engineers first needed one ingredient: how do the labor hours a run consumes depend on the size of the lot?

They pulled records from 25 recent runs made under stable conditions over a six-month period. Each record is a pair: the lot size (units produced) and the work hours the run took. The lot sizes are all multiples of ten, a scheduling convenience, and they range from 20 to 120 units. The scatter of these 25 points is the starting picture of the whole chapter.

Two things stand out in Figure 1. Bigger lots take more hours, and the cloud of points is close enough to a straight line that a line is a reasonable summary. But which line? An engineer could lay a ruler on the plot and draw one by eye, and a second engineer would draw a slightly different one. This chapter replaces the ruler with a rule: a precise, defensible recipe for the single best line, an honest account of how much to trust it, and the assumptions that make the whole enterprise valid. By the end you will be able to fit that line, read its slope in the units of the problem (hours per unit of lot size), say how uncertain the slope is, and prove that under stated conditions no competing method does better.

This lesson at a glance

  • What we are doing: Fitting the single best straight line to the Toluca lot-size versus work-hours data by least squares, and proving the properties that make it trustworthy.

  • Why we are doing it: A line drawn by eye is arbitrary; we need a precise, defensible recipe for the one best line and an honest account of how much to trust its slope.

  • Main objective: State the simple linear regression model, derive and compute the least-squares estimates b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​, and prove why they are the best linear unbiased estimators.

  • What changed from the last chapters: Chapter 1 argued that regression is a way of thinking; from here it becomes a computable method. This is the first full pass around the ASK-EXPLORE-FIT-CHECK-USE workflow (The modeling workflow) that this chapter names.

Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

  • State the simple linear regression model and its assumptions, and explain the job each assumption does.

  • Derive the least-squares estimators b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ two ways: by calculus and by an algebraic identity.

  • Compute b0b_0b0​, b1b_1b1​, fitted values, and residuals by hand on a small dataset and with software on the full one.

  • Prove the algebraic properties of residuals and use them to check a fitted model.

  • Explain why the error variance is estimated with the divisor n−2n-2n−2, deriving E{MSE}=σ2E\{\mathrm{MSE}\} = \sigma^2E{MSE}=σ2, and compute MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE and sss.

  • Derive the means and variances of b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​, and prove the Gauss-Markov result that b1b_1b1​ is the best linear unbiased estimator.

  • Show that maximum likelihood under normal errors reproduces the least-squares estimates.

The modeling workflow¶

Every chapter of this book is one pass through the same five-stage loop. Naming the stages now gives you a map to carry through the whole course, and every later chapter opens by saying which stage it serves.

  • ASK. Fix the question and the data that can answer it. Here: how do work hours depend on lot size, and what can 25 production runs tell us?

  • EXPLORE. Plot and summarize before fitting anything. The scatter in Figure 1 is this stage; it is what tells us a straight line is even worth trying.

  • FIT. Estimate the model. Most of this chapter lives here, turning the ruler-and-eye line into the single least-squares line.

  • CHECK. Ask whether the fitted model can be trusted, using the residuals and the assumptions behind them. We begin this in Section 2.3 and devote all of Chapter 9 to it.

  • USE. Interpret the estimates, predict, and decide. Reading the slope in hours per unit of lot size is the first taste; inference and prediction fill Chapter 3.

As Figure 2 shows, the stages form a loop, not a one-way street: a failed CHECK sends you back to EXPLORE or FIT with a better model. Simple linear regression is the smallest complete trip around this loop, which is why the course starts here.

2.1 The simple linear regression model¶

Intuition¶

Regression starts from a plain idea: one thing tends to move with another, and we want to pin that relationship down in numbers. Here we describe how a response YYY (Toluca work hours) depends on a single predictor XXX (lot size). No sane model claims the hours are an exact function of lot size: two runs of the same size took different amounts of time, because of tool wear, the crew on shift, the weather, and a hundred small things nobody recorded. So we split each observation into two pieces: a systematic part that lot size explains, and a random part that it does not.

The systematic part is a straight line. On average, a run of size XXX takes some baseline amount of time plus a fixed number of extra hours per additional unit. The random part is a disturbance that pushes the actual hours above or below that average. We assume the disturbance has no built-in tendency to be positive or negative, has the same typical size regardless of lot size, and does not coordinate from one run to the next.

Formula¶

The simple linear regression model (Definition 2.1) for observations i=1,…,ni = 1, \dots, ni=1,…,n is

Yi=β0+β1Xi+εi.Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i .Yi​=β0​+β1​Xi​+εi​.
Definition 2.1: Simple linear regression model

For cases i=1,…,ni = 1, \dots, ni=1,…,n, the response, predictor, and error are related by Yi=β0+β1Xi+εiY_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​Xi​+εi​, where β0\beta_0β0​ (intercept) and β1\beta_1β1​ (slope) are unknown constants, each XiX_iXi​ is a known constant, and the errors satisfy E{εi}=0E\{\varepsilon_i\} = 0E{εi​}=0, Var⁡{εi}=σ2\operatorname{Var}\{\varepsilon_i\} = \sigma^2Var{εi​}=σ2, and Cov⁡{εi,εj}=0\operatorname{Cov}\{\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j\} = 0Cov{εi​,εj​}=0 for i≠ji \neq ji=j.

  • YiY_iYi​ is the observed response in the iii-th case (work hours for run iii).

  • XiX_iXi​ is the predictor in the iii-th case (lot size for run iii), treated as a known, fixed constant. Some books call this the independent variable or the explanatory variable; this book says predictor throughout.

  • β0\beta_0β0​ is the intercept parameter: the mean response when X=0X = 0X=0.

  • β1\beta_1β1​ is the slope parameter: the change in the mean response for a one-unit increase in XXX.

  • εi\varepsilon_iεi​ is the random error in the iii-th case, the amount by which YiY_iYi​ departs from its mean.

The parameters β0\beta_0β0​ and β1\beta_1β1​ are fixed numbers we do not know and want to estimate. The model puts four conditions on the errors:

E{εi}=0,Var⁡{εi}=σ2,Cov⁡{εi,εj}=0 (i≠j).E\{\varepsilon_i\} = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}\{\varepsilon_i\} = \sigma^2, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}\{\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j\} = 0 \ (i \neq j).E{εi​}=0,Var{εi​}=σ2,Cov{εi​,εj​}=0 (i=j).

In words: each error averages to zero (the line is right on average), every error has the same variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 (constant spread, called homoscedasticity), and distinct errors are uncorrelated (one run’s luck says nothing about another’s). Notice what is not yet assumed: no particular shape for the error distribution. Normality enters only in 2.6 Maximum likelihood under normal errors, and only when we want to build intervals and tests.

Because XiX_iXi​ is a fixed constant and β0+β1Xi\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_iβ0​+β1​Xi​ is therefore also constant, the error conditions transfer directly to the responses:

E{Yi}=β0+β1Xi,Var⁡{Yi}=σ2.E\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i, \qquad \operatorname{Var}\{Y_i\} = \sigma^2 .E{Yi​}=β0​+β1​Xi​,Var{Yi​}=σ2.

The quantity E{Yi}E\{Y_i\}E{Yi​} is the mean response at level XiX_iXi​. The function E{Y}=β0+β1XE\{Y\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 XE{Y}=β0​+β1​X that gives the mean response at any XXX is the regression function (Definition 2.2). It is a line, and estimating it is the whole game.

Definition 2.2: Regression function

The regression function is the mean response as a function of the predictor, E{Y}=β0+β1XE\{Y\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 XE{Y}=β0​+β1​X. In simple linear regression it is a straight line, and estimating it is the goal of the whole chapter.

Figure 3 is the mental picture to carry through the chapter: a straight mean line, with a distribution of possible YYY values stacked at each XXX, every stack the same width.

A note on symbols

Throughout the book, Greek letters (β0,β1,σ2\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2β0​,β1​,σ2) are unknown population parameters, and Roman letters (b0,b1,s2b_0, b_1, s^2b0​,b1​,s2) are the estimates we compute from data. A hat means an estimate or a prediction, so β^0\hat\beta_0β^​0​ and b0b_0b0​ are two names for the same thing, and Y^i\hat{Y}_iY^i​ is the estimated mean response. We write the normal distribution as N(μ,σ2)N(\mu, \sigma^2)N(μ,σ2), with the variance in the second slot.

Try it 2.1

A classmate says “the model assumes YYY is a straight-line function of XXX.” Correct the statement so it is accurate, and name the assumption that the classmate dropped.

Solution

The model does not say YYY is a straight-line function of XXX; it says the mean of YYY is a straight-line function of XXX, that is E{Yi}=β0+β1XiE\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_iE{Yi​}=β0​+β1​Xi​. Any individual YiY_iYi​ sits off the line by the random error εi\varepsilon_iεi​. The dropped piece is the error term and its conditions, especially constant variance Var⁡{εi}=σ2\operatorname{Var}\{\varepsilon_i\} = \sigma^2Var{εi​}=σ2: the points scatter around the line by the same amount at every XXX.

2.2 Least squares from first principles¶

Intuition¶

We have a cloud of points and want the one line that fits best. “Best” needs a definition. Least squares defines it by penalizing misses: for a candidate line, measure the vertical gap from each point to the line, square the gaps so that overshooting and undershooting both count as errors and large misses hurt disproportionately, and add them up. The best line is the one that makes this total, the sum of squared errors, as small as possible. Figure 4 shows the idea with three candidate lines through the Toluca data.

Formula¶

Write a candidate line with intercept b0b_0b0​ and slope b1b_1b1​. Its sum of squared errors (Definition 2.3) is

Q(b0,b1)=∑i=1n(Yi−b0−b1Xi)2.Q(b_0, b_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i \right)^2 .Q(b0​,b1​)=i=1∑n​(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)2.

  • Yi−b0−b1XiY_i - b_0 - b_1 X_iYi​−b0​−b1​Xi​ is the vertical gap from the point (Xi,Yi)(X_i, Y_i)(Xi​,Yi​) to the candidate line.

  • QQQ is a function of the two numbers b0,b1b_0, b_1b0​,b1​ we get to choose; the data are fixed.

Definition 2.3: Least-squares criterion

For a candidate line with intercept b0b_0b0​ and slope b1b_1b1​, the sum of squared errors is Q(b0,b1)=∑i=1n(Yi−b0−b1Xi)2Q(b_0, b_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i)^2Q(b0​,b1​)=∑i=1n​(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)2. The least-squares estimates are the values of b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ that minimize QQQ.

The least-squares estimates b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ are the values that minimize QQQ. To write them compactly, define the three basic sums of squares and cross-products around the means:

Sxx=∑i=1n(Xi−Xˉ)2,Sxy=∑i=1n(Xi−Xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ),Syy=∑i=1n(Yi−Yˉ)2,S_{xx} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - \bar{X})^2, \qquad S_{xy} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y}), \qquad S_{yy} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \bar{Y})^2,Sxx​=i=1∑n​(Xi​−Xˉ)2,Sxy​=i=1∑n​(Xi​−Xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ),Syy​=i=1∑n​(Yi​−Yˉ)2,

where Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ and Yˉ\bar{Y}Yˉ are the sample means of the predictor and response. The next two derivations establish the minimizers, stated here first.

Theorem 2.4: Least-squares estimates

Under the simple linear regression model, if the XiX_iXi​ are not all equal, the sum of squares Q(b0,b1)Q(b_0, b_1)Q(b0​,b1​) has a unique minimizer, the least-squares estimates

b1=SxySxx,b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉ.b_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}, \qquad b_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1 \bar{X} .b1​=Sxx​Sxy​​,b0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ.

Derivation by calculus¶

Proof (by calculus). Q(b0,b1)Q(b_0, b_1)Q(b0​,b1​) is a sum of squares, so it is smooth and bounded below by zero. At a minimum, both partial derivatives vanish. Differentiate:

∂Q∂b0=∑i=1n2(Yi−b0−b1Xi)(−1),∂Q∂b1=∑i=1n2(Yi−b0−b1Xi)(−Xi).\frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_0} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\left(Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i\right)(-1), \qquad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial b_1} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} 2\left(Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i\right)(-X_i).∂b0​∂Q​=i=1∑n​2(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)(−1),∂b1​∂Q​=i=1∑n​2(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)(−Xi​).

Setting each to zero and dividing by -2 gives the normal equations:

∑i=1n(Yi−b0−b1Xi)=0,∑i=1nXi(Yi−b0−b1Xi)=0.\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i\right) = 0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\left(Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i\right) = 0 .i=1∑n​(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)=0,i=1∑n​Xi​(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)=0.

Expand the sums. The first equation becomes ∑Yi=nb0+b1∑Xi\sum Y_i = n b_0 + b_1 \sum X_i∑Yi​=nb0​+b1​∑Xi​, and dividing by nnn gives Yˉ=b0+b1Xˉ\bar{Y} = b_0 + b_1 \bar{X}Yˉ=b0​+b1​Xˉ, so

b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉ.b_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1 \bar{X}.b0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ.

Substitute this into the second normal equation ∑XiYi=b0∑Xi+b1∑Xi2\sum X_i Y_i = b_0 \sum X_i + b_1 \sum X_i^2∑Xi​Yi​=b0​∑Xi​+b1​∑Xi2​. Replacing b0b_0b0​ and collecting the b1b_1b1​ terms,

∑XiYi−Yˉ∑Xi=b1(∑Xi2−Xˉ∑Xi).\sum X_i Y_i - \bar{Y}\sum X_i = b_1\left(\sum X_i^2 - \bar{X}\sum X_i\right).∑Xi​Yi​−Yˉ∑Xi​=b1​(∑Xi2​−Xˉ∑Xi​).

The left side equals ∑XiYi−nXˉYˉ=∑(Xi−Xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)=Sxy\sum X_i Y_i - n \bar{X}\bar{Y} = \sum (X_i - \bar X)(Y_i - \bar Y) = S_{xy}∑Xi​Yi​−nXˉYˉ=∑(Xi​−Xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)=Sxy​, and the right side’s bracket equals ∑Xi2−nXˉ2=∑(Xi−Xˉ)2=Sxx\sum X_i^2 - n\bar{X}^2 = \sum (X_i - \bar X)^2 = S_{xx}∑Xi2​−nXˉ2=∑(Xi​−Xˉ)2=Sxx​. Therefore

b1=SxySxx.b_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} .b1​=Sxx​Sxy​​.

This is the only stationary point, and it is a minimum by the second-derivatives test for a function of two variables (the same test you would use in calculus for one variable, extended to two). The three second partial derivatives of QQQ are constants: Qb0b0=2nQ_{b_0 b_0} = 2nQb0​b0​​=2n, Qb1b1=2∑Xi2Q_{b_1 b_1} = 2\sum X_i^2Qb1​b1​​=2∑Xi2​, and Qb0b1=2∑XiQ_{b_0 b_1} = 2\sum X_iQb0​b1​​=2∑Xi​. Form the test quantity D=Qb0b0 Qb1b1−(Qb0b1)2=4(n∑Xi2−(∑Xi)2)=4n SxxD = Q_{b_0 b_0}\,Q_{b_1 b_1} - (Q_{b_0 b_1})^2 = 4\big(n\sum X_i^2 - (\sum X_i)^2\big) = 4n\,S_{xx}D=Qb0​b0​​Qb1​b1​​−(Qb0​b1​​)2=4(n∑Xi2​−(∑Xi​)2)=4nSxx​. Since D>0D > 0D>0 whenever the XiX_iXi​ are not all equal, and Qb0b0=2n>0Q_{b_0 b_0} = 2n > 0Qb0​b0​​=2n>0, the stationary point is a local minimum. Because QQQ is a sum of squares (so it is bounded below by zero) and this is its only stationary point, that local minimum is also the global minimum. (Chapter 7 revisits this same fact in matrix form, once you have the tools of Chapter 6.) ■\blacksquare■

Derivation by an algebraic identity¶

The calculus argument finds the minimizer but leaves the geometry a little hidden. Here is a second proof that uses no derivatives and shows directly that no line beats the least-squares line. It rests on two facts we will prove in 2.3 Fitted values and the properties of residuals: writing the fitted values as Y^i=b0+b1Xi\hat{Y}_i = b_0 + b_1 X_iY^i​=b0​+b1​Xi​ and the residuals as ei=Yi−Y^ie_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_iei​=Yi​−Y^i​, the residuals satisfy ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0 and ∑Xiei=0\sum X_i e_i = 0∑Xi​ei​=0.

Proof (by an algebraic identity). Take any competing line with intercept aaa and slope ccc. Split the gap from each point to that line by routing it through the least-squares fitted value:

Yi−a−cXi=(Yi−Y^i)⏟ei+(Y^i−a−cXi)⏟gi,gi=(b0−a)+(b1−c)Xi.Y_i - a - c X_i = \underbrace{(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)}_{e_i} + \underbrace{(\hat{Y}_i - a - c X_i)}_{g_i}, \qquad g_i = (b_0 - a) + (b_1 - c) X_i .Yi​−a−cXi​=ei​(Yi​−Y^i​)​​+gi​(Y^i​−a−cXi​)​​,gi​=(b0​−a)+(b1​−c)Xi​.

Square and sum. The sum of squared errors for the competing line is

∑(Yi−a−cXi)2=∑ei2+∑gi2+2∑eigi.\sum \left(Y_i - a - c X_i\right)^2 = \sum e_i^2 + \sum g_i^2 + 2 \sum e_i g_i .∑(Yi​−a−cXi​)2=∑ei2​+∑gi2​+2∑ei​gi​.

The cross term vanishes:

∑eigi=(b0−a)∑ei+(b1−c)∑Xiei=(b0−a)⋅0+(b1−c)⋅0=0.\sum e_i g_i = (b_0 - a)\sum e_i + (b_1 - c)\sum X_i e_i = (b_0 - a)\cdot 0 + (b_1 - c)\cdot 0 = 0 .∑ei​gi​=(b0​−a)∑ei​+(b1​−c)∑Xi​ei​=(b0​−a)⋅0+(b1​−c)⋅0=0.

So for every competing line,

∑(Yi−a−cXi)2=∑ei2⏟SSE of the LS line+∑gi2  ≥  ∑ei2,\sum \left(Y_i - a - c X_i\right)^2 = \underbrace{\sum e_i^2}_{\text{SSE of the LS line}} + \sum g_i^2 \; \ge \; \sum e_i^2 ,∑(Yi​−a−cXi​)2=SSE of the LS line∑ei2​​​+∑gi2​≥∑ei2​,

with equality only when ∑gi2=0\sum g_i^2 = 0∑gi2​=0, that is when gi=0g_i = 0gi​=0 for all iii, which (since the XiX_iXi​ are not all equal) forces a=b0a = b_0a=b0​ and c=b1c = b_1c=b1​. The least-squares line is the unique minimizer. ■\blacksquare■

The two normal equations have a clean picture. Each one is a line in the (b0,b1)(b_0, b_1)(b0​,b1​) plane, and the least-squares estimates sit where they cross, at the bottom of the SSE bowl. Figure 5 shows the bowl and Figure 6 shows it from above.

Key idea

Because QQQ is a sum of squares, it is a convex bowl with exactly one lowest point. Least squares therefore always has a single, unambiguous answer: there are no rival valleys to get trapped in, and the two normal equations pin down that one point.

R¶

Fitting the model in R uses lm, which reads a formula response ~ predictor. First read the data and look at it.

toluca <- read.csv("data/toluca.csv")
dim(toluca)
head(toluca, 3)
[1] 25  2
  lotsize hours
1      80   399
2      30   121
3      50   221
Example 2.1: The Toluca least-squares line

Question. What straight line best predicts work hours from lot size, and how many hours does the model expect for a lot of 65 units?

Intuition. Fit the line that minimizes the total squared vertical gap, then read off its intercept and slope, and plug in X=65X = 65X=65.

Formula. b1=Sxy/Sxxb_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}b1​=Sxy​/Sxx​, b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉb_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1\bar{X}b0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ, and the point estimate of the mean response at X=65X = 65X=65 is Y^=b0+b1(65)\hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1(65)Y^=b0​+b1​(65).

Computation.

fit <- lm(hours ~ lotsize, data = toluca)
coef(fit)
predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(lotsize = 65))
(Intercept)     lotsize
  62.365859    3.570202
      1
  294.429

The same numbers come straight out of the sums SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ and SxyS_{xy}Sxy​, confirming the formulas:

x <- toluca$lotsize
y <- toluca$hours
Sxx <- sum((x - mean(x))^2)
Sxy <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y)))
b1 <- Sxy / Sxx
b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x)
round(c(Sxx = Sxx, Sxy = Sxy, b0 = b0, b1 = b1), 4)
       Sxx        Sxy         b0         b1
19800.0000 70690.0000    62.3659     3.5702

Now in Python, with statsmodels’ formula interface reading the same CSV.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

toluca = pd.read_csv("data/toluca.csv")
fit = smf.ols("hours ~ lotsize", data=toluca).fit()
print(fit.params)
print(fit.predict(pd.DataFrame({"lotsize": [65]})))
Intercept    62.365859
lotsize       3.570202
dtype: float64
0    294.42899
dtype: float64
x = toluca["lotsize"]
y = toluca["hours"]
Sxx = np.sum((x - x.mean()) ** 2)
Sxy = np.sum((x - x.mean()) * (y - y.mean()))
b1 = Sxy / Sxx
b0 = y.mean() - b1 * x.mean()
print(round(Sxx, 4), round(Sxy, 4), round(b0, 4), round(b1, 4))
19800.0 70690.0 62.3659 3.5702

Interpretation. The fitted line is Y^=62.37+3.5702 X\hat{Y} = 62.37 + 3.5702\,XY^=62.37+3.5702X. The slope says that each extra unit in a lot adds about 3.57 work hours on average, over the observed range of lot sizes (20 to 120). The intercept 62.37 is the model’s mean hours at a lot size of zero; since no lot is anywhere near zero units, treat it as a mathematical anchor for the line, not a physically meaningful “hours to make nothing.” For a lot of 65 units the model expects about 294 work hours.

Being able to reproduce lm from the raw sums SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ and SxyS_{xy}Sxy​ matters: it means you can compute a regression anywhere, check software output, and, later, extend the idea when there is no lm button for the model you need.

Durable skill: Turn a vague goal into an optimization

“Fit the best line” is not yet a math problem; “choose b0,b1b_0, b_1b0​,b1​ to minimize ∑(Yi−b0−b1Xi)2\sum (Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i)^2∑(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)2” is. The move that made regression tractable, naming a precise loss and minimizing it, is the same move behind most of modern statistics and machine learning. When you meet a new method, ask first: what quantity is it minimizing, and why that one? To practice, take any “find the best” task you meet this term and write down the objective function before you touch software.

Small datasets are worth computing by hand once, so the formulas stop being black boxes. The file toluca_mini.csv is a six-row slice of the Toluca data, small enough to do on paper. Figure 7 shows its points and their deviations from the means, the raw material of SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ and SxyS_{xy}Sxy​.

Example 2.2: Computing the estimates by hand

Question. On the six-run mini dataset, find b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ from the deviation sums.

Intuition. With only six rows you can compute Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ, Yˉ\bar{Y}Yˉ, then each deviation and cross-product, then SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ and SxyS_{xy}Sxy​, and finally the two estimates.

Formula. b1=Sxy/Sxxb_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}b1​=Sxy​/Sxx​ and b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉb_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1\bar{X}b0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ, exactly as before.

Computation.

mini <- read.csv("data/toluca_mini.csv")
xm <- mini$lotsize
ym <- mini$hours
Sxx_m <- sum((xm - mean(xm))^2)
Sxy_m <- sum((xm - mean(xm)) * (ym - mean(ym)))
b1_m <- Sxy_m / Sxx_m
b0_m <- mean(ym) - b1_m * mean(xm)
round(c(xbar = mean(xm), ybar = mean(ym),
        Sxx = Sxx_m, Sxy = Sxy_m, b0 = b0_m, b1 = b1_m), 4)
     xbar      ybar       Sxx       Sxy        b0        b1
  81.6667  332.6667 1883.3333 7893.3333   -9.6106    4.1912
mini = pd.read_csv("data/toluca_mini.csv")
xm = mini["lotsize"]
ym = mini["hours"]
Sxx_m = np.sum((xm - xm.mean()) ** 2)
Sxy_m = np.sum((xm - xm.mean()) * (ym - ym.mean()))
b1_m = Sxy_m / Sxx_m
b0_m = ym.mean() - b1_m * xm.mean()
print(round(xm.mean(), 4), round(ym.mean(), 4),
      round(Sxx_m, 4), round(Sxy_m, 4),
      round(b0_m, 4), round(b1_m, 4))
81.6667 332.6667 1883.3333 7893.3333 -9.6106 4.1912

Interpretation. By hand the six-run fit is Y^=−9.61+4.19 X\hat{Y} = -9.61 + 4.19\,XY^=−9.61+4.19X. The slope 4.19 is in the same ballpark as the full data’s 3.57, but not equal, and the intercept swings negative: six points pin a line far less firmly than 25, a first hint of the sampling variability that the rest of the chapter quantifies. The lesson is not that the small answer is wrong, it is that a slope estimate always comes with uncertainty, and less data means more of it.

Try it 2.2

Using the printed sums in Example 2.2 (Sxx=1883.33S_{xx} = 1883.33Sxx​=1883.33, Sxy=7893.33S_{xy} = 7893.33Sxy​=7893.33, Xˉ=81.67\bar{X} = 81.67Xˉ=81.67, Yˉ=332.67\bar{Y} = 332.67Yˉ=332.67), reproduce b1b_1b1​ and b0b_0b0​ with a calculator, then predict the work hours for a lot of 100 units.

Solution

b1=Sxy/Sxx=7893.33/1883.33=4.1912b_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx} = 7893.33 / 1883.33 = 4.1912b1​=Sxy​/Sxx​=7893.33/1883.33=4.1912. Then b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉ=332.67−4.1912(81.67)=−9.61b_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1\bar{X} = 332.67 - 4.1912(81.67) = -9.61b0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ=332.67−4.1912(81.67)=−9.61. The prediction at X=100X = 100X=100 is Y^=−9.61+4.1912(100)=409.5\hat{Y} = -9.61 + 4.1912(100) = 409.5Y^=−9.61+4.1912(100)=409.5 hours. (The full 25-run model would predict 62.37+3.5702(100)=419.462.37 + 3.5702(100) = 419.462.37+3.5702(100)=419.4 hours; the two disagree because six points estimate the line loosely.)

Before you take the formulas on trust, spend a minute trying to beat them by hand.

What to notice. No pair of slider settings pushes QQQ below 54,825.554{,}825.554,825.5, and the settings that come closest read 62.5 and 3.57, the least-squares estimates. Try this. Hold the slope at 3.57 and sweep the intercept alone: the sum of residuals crosses zero at exactly the setting where QQQ bottoms out, which is the first normal equation happening in front of you. Back to Section 2.2.

2.3 Fitted values and the properties of residuals¶

Intuition¶

Once the line is fixed, every observed point splits into two parts. The fitted value Y^i\hat{Y}_iY^i​ (Definition 2.5) is where the line says the point should be; the residual ei=Yi−Y^ie_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_iei​=Yi​−Y^i​ is how far the actual point lands from it. Residuals are the model’s leftovers, the part of YYY that lot size did not explain. Figure 9 draws them as the vertical sticks connecting each point to the line. They are not just scenery: least squares forces the residuals to satisfy exact algebraic identities, and those identities are both a proof tool and a practical way to catch a mistake in a fit.

Formula¶

The fitted values and residuals are

Y^i=b0+b1Xi,ei=Yi−Y^i.\hat{Y}_i = b_0 + b_1 X_i, \qquad e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i .Y^i​=b0​+b1​Xi​,ei​=Yi​−Y^i​.

  • Y^i\hat{Y}_iY^i​ is the estimated mean response at XiX_iXi​, the height of the fitted line there.

  • eie_iei​ is the residual, the vertical gap from the observed YiY_iYi​ down to the line.

Definition 2.5: Fitted values and residuals

The fitted value at XiX_iXi​ is Y^i=b0+b1Xi\hat{Y}_i = b_0 + b_1 X_iY^i​=b0​+b1​Xi​, the height of the least-squares line there. The residual is ei=Yi−Y^ie_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_iei​=Yi​−Y^i​, the signed vertical gap from the observed point to that line.

Do not confuse eie_iei​ with the model error εi=Yi−(β0+β1Xi)\varepsilon_i = Y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i)εi​=Yi​−(β0​+β1​Xi​). The error is the gap to the true, unknown line; the residual is the gap to our estimated line. We never see εi\varepsilon_iεi​, but we can always compute eie_iei​, and it is our best stand-in. Figure 10 puts the two gaps side by side so the difference is impossible to miss.

Derivation (properties of residuals)¶

Theorem 2.6: Algebraic properties of the residuals

For the least-squares fit of a model with an intercept, the residuals satisfy

∑i=1nei=0,∑i=1nXiei=0,∑i=1nY^iei=0,∑i=1nY^i=∑i=1nYi,\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i = 0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i e_i = 0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{Y}_i e_i = 0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{Y}_i = \sum_{i=1}^{n} Y_i,i=1∑n​ei​=0,i=1∑n​Xi​ei​=0,i=1∑n​Y^i​ei​=0,i=1∑n​Y^i​=i=1∑n​Yi​,

and the fitted line passes through the point of means (Xˉ,Yˉ)(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})(Xˉ,Yˉ).

Proof. All of these follow from the two normal equations of 2.2 Least squares from first principles.

  1. The residuals sum to zero. The first normal equation is exactly ∑(Yi−b0−b1Xi)=∑ei=0\sum (Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i) = \sum e_i = 0∑(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)=∑ei​=0.

  2. The predictor is orthogonal to the residuals. The second normal equation is exactly ∑Xi(Yi−b0−b1Xi)=∑Xiei=0\sum X_i (Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i) = \sum X_i e_i = 0∑Xi​(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)=∑Xi​ei​=0.

  3. The fitted values are orthogonal to the residuals. Using properties 1 and 2, ∑Y^iei=∑(b0+b1Xi)ei=b0∑ei+b1∑Xiei=0\sum \hat{Y}_i e_i = \sum (b_0 + b_1 X_i) e_i = b_0 \sum e_i + b_1 \sum X_i e_i = 0∑Y^i​ei​=∑(b0​+b1​Xi​)ei​=b0​∑ei​+b1​∑Xi​ei​=0.

  4. The fitted values reproduce the total of YYY. From property 1, ∑ei=∑(Yi−Y^i)=0\sum e_i = \sum (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i) = 0∑ei​=∑(Yi​−Y^i​)=0, so ∑Y^i=∑Yi\sum \hat{Y}_i = \sum Y_i∑Y^i​=∑Yi​, and dividing by nnn, the mean fitted value equals Yˉ\bar{Y}Yˉ.

  5. The line passes through the center of the data. Setting X=XˉX = \bar{X}X=Xˉ in the fitted line and using b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉb_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1 \bar{X}b0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ gives Y^=b0+b1Xˉ=Yˉ\hat{Y} = b_0 + b_1 \bar{X} = \bar{Y}Y^=b0​+b1​Xˉ=Yˉ. So (Xˉ,Yˉ)(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})(Xˉ,Yˉ) is always on the least-squares line. ■\blacksquare■

Property 1 is why the vertical sticks in Figure 9 balance out. Properties 1 and 2 were the ingredients that made the cross term vanish in the algebraic proof of 2.2 Least squares from first principles, so the identities repay the loan we took there.

R and Python¶

Example 2.3: Checking the residual identities

Question. Do the Toluca residuals really satisfy ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0, ∑Xiei=0\sum X_i e_i = 0∑Xi​ei​=0, ∑Y^iei=0\sum \hat{Y}_i e_i = 0∑Y^i​ei​=0, and ∑Y^i=∑Yi\sum \hat{Y}_i = \sum Y_i∑Y^i​=∑Yi​?

Intuition. Compute the residuals and fitted values from the fitted model and evaluate the four sums. They should be zero (up to floating-point dust) and matching.

Formula. The four identities of the derivation above.

Computation.

e <- residuals(fit)
yhat <- fitted(fit)
round(c(sum_e = sum(e),
        sum_x_times_e = sum(x * e),
        sum_yhat_times_e = sum(yhat * e)), 8)
round(c(sum_y = sum(y), sum_yhat = sum(yhat)), 4)
           sum_e    sum_x_times_e sum_yhat_times_e
               0                0                0
   sum_y sum_yhat
    7807     7807
e = fit.resid
yhat = fit.fittedvalues
print(round(np.sum(e), 8),
      round(np.sum(x * e), 8),
      round(np.sum(yhat * e), 8))
print(round(np.sum(y), 4), round(np.sum(yhat), 4))
-0.0 -0.0 -0.0
7807 7807.0

Interpretation. All three orthogonality sums are zero (the -0.0 in Python is floating-point for exactly zero), and the fitted values total 7807, the same as the observed hours. The identities hold, as they must for any correct least-squares fit. If you ever compute a fit by hand and ∑ei\sum e_i∑ei​ is not zero, you have made an arithmetic error, no diagnostics needed.

A plot of the residuals against the predictor is the first picture to draw after any fit. If the model’s constant-variance and straight-line assumptions hold, the residuals should hover around zero with no trend and no fanning, as in Figure 11. A curve would signal that the relationship is not straight; a widening funnel would signal nonconstant variance. Chapter 9 builds a full diagnostic toolkit on this one habit.

Try it 2.3

A colleague reports a fitted line for which the residuals sum to 14, not zero, and insists the fit is least squares. Without seeing the data, what can you conclude?

Solution

The fit cannot be the least-squares fit of a model that includes an intercept. Property 1 says ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0 exactly for the least-squares line, as a consequence of the first normal equation. A nonzero residual sum means either the intercept was forced to some fixed value (a no-intercept or constrained fit), or the coefficients are simply not the least-squares ones, or there is an arithmetic error. In every case the reported line is not the ordinary least-squares fit.

The identities in Theorem 2.6 are exact, so the fastest way to believe them is to try to break one.

What to notice. However badly you mangle the data, ∑ei\sum e_i∑ei​ and ∑Xiei\sum X_i e_i∑Xi​ei​ stay at zero and the mean of Y^\hat{Y}Y^ stays equal to Yˉ\bar{Y}Yˉ. Try this. Drag one run to the very top of the plot: the residuals become huge, the fit becomes useless, and the identities do not move, which is why they check your arithmetic and never your model. Back to Section 2.3.

2.4 Estimating the error variance¶

Intuition¶

The slope and intercept describe the line, but the model has a third unknown: σ2\sigma^2σ2, the variance of the errors, which controls how tightly the points hug the line. A small σ2\sigma^2σ2 means predictions can be sharp; a large one means even a perfect line leaves big uncertainty. We cannot see the errors εi\varepsilon_iεi​, but the residuals eie_iei​ are their visible stand-ins, so we estimate σ2\sigma^2σ2 from the spread of the residuals. Figure 13 shows what that spread looks like as a band around the fitted line.

Formula¶

The error sum of squares (Definition 2.7) and the estimator of σ2\sigma^2σ2 are

SSE=∑i=1nei2=∑i=1n(Yi−Y^i)2,s2=MSE=SSEn−2,s=MSE.\mathrm{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2, \qquad s^2 = \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-2}, \qquad s = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}} .SSE=i=1∑n​ei2​=i=1∑n​(Yi​−Y^i​)2,s2=MSE=n−2SSE​,s=MSE​.

  • SSE\mathrm{SSE}SSE is the total squared residual, the leftover variation the line did not explain.

  • MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE (mean square error), also written s2s^2s2, is SSE\mathrm{SSE}SSE divided by its degrees of freedom n−2n-2n−2; it estimates σ2\sigma^2σ2.

  • sss is the estimated standard deviation of the errors, in the units of YYY (hours).

Definition 2.7: Error sum of squares and mean square error

The error sum of squares is SSE=∑i=1nei2\mathrm{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2SSE=∑i=1n​ei2​. The mean square error s2=MSE=SSE/(n−2)s^2 = \mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)s2=MSE=SSE/(n−2) estimates the error variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, and s=MSEs = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}}s=MSE​ estimates the error standard deviation, in the units of YYY.

The divisor is n−2n-2n−2, not nnn or n−1n-1n−1. Two degrees of freedom are spent estimating the two coefficients b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ that define the line the residuals are measured from. The next derivation shows that this exact divisor, and no other, makes MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE correct on average.

Derivation (why the divisor is n−2n-2n−2)¶

Theorem 2.8: Unbiasedness of the mean square error

Under the simple linear regression model, E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2E\{\mathrm{SSE}\} = (n-2)\sigma^2E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2, so that E{MSE}=σ2E\{\mathrm{MSE}\} = \sigma^2E{MSE}=σ2. The divisor n−2n-2n−2 is exactly what makes MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE an unbiased estimator of the error variance.

Proof. We show E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2E\{\mathrm{SSE}\} = (n-2)\sigma^2E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2, so that dividing by n−2n-2n−2 gives an estimator that is right on average. Start from a tidy identity for SSE. Since Y^i=Yˉ+b1(Xi−Xˉ)\hat{Y}_i = \bar{Y} + b_1(X_i - \bar{X})Y^i​=Yˉ+b1​(Xi​−Xˉ) (using b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉb_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1 \bar Xb0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ),

ei=Yi−Y^i=(Yi−Yˉ)−b1(Xi−Xˉ),e_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_i = (Y_i - \bar{Y}) - b_1 (X_i - \bar{X}),ei​=Yi​−Y^i​=(Yi​−Yˉ)−b1​(Xi​−Xˉ),

so, expanding the square and using Sxy=b1SxxS_{xy} = b_1 S_{xx}Sxy​=b1​Sxx​,

SSE=∑ei2=Syy−2b1Sxy+b12Sxx=Syy−2b1(b1Sxx)+b12Sxx=Syy−b12Sxx.\mathrm{SSE} = \sum e_i^2 = S_{yy} - 2 b_1 S_{xy} + b_1^2 S_{xx} = S_{yy} - 2 b_1 (b_1 S_{xx}) + b_1^2 S_{xx} = S_{yy} - b_1^2 S_{xx}.SSE=∑ei2​=Syy​−2b1​Sxy​+b12​Sxx​=Syy​−2b1​(b1​Sxx​)+b12​Sxx​=Syy​−b12​Sxx​.

Take expectations of the two pieces. For any random variable, E{W2}=Var⁡{W}+(E{W})2E\{W^2\} = \operatorname{Var}\{W\} + (E\{W\})^2E{W2}=Var{W}+(E{W})2.

The slope piece. We show in 2.5 Sampling behavior and the Gauss-Markov theorem that E{b1}=β1E\{b_1\} = \beta_1E{b1​}=β1​ and Var⁡{b1}=σ2/Sxx\operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} = \sigma^2 / S_{xx}Var{b1​}=σ2/Sxx​. Hence

E{b12Sxx}=Sxx(Var⁡{b1}+(E{b1})2)=Sxx(σ2Sxx+β12)=σ2+β12Sxx.E\{b_1^2 S_{xx}\} = S_{xx}\left(\operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} + (E\{b_1\})^2\right) = S_{xx}\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} + \beta_1^2\right) = \sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}.E{b12​Sxx​}=Sxx​(Var{b1​}+(E{b1​})2)=Sxx​(Sxx​σ2​+β12​)=σ2+β12​Sxx​.

The total piece. Write Syy=∑Yi2−nYˉ2S_{yy} = \sum Y_i^2 - n\bar{Y}^2Syy​=∑Yi2​−nYˉ2. Each YiY_iYi​ has mean μi=β0+β1Xi\mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_iμi​=β0​+β1​Xi​ and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, so E{Yi2}=σ2+μi2E\{Y_i^2\} = \sigma^2 + \mu_i^2E{Yi2​}=σ2+μi2​ and E{∑Yi2}=nσ2+∑μi2E\{\sum Y_i^2\} = n\sigma^2 + \sum \mu_i^2E{∑Yi2​}=nσ2+∑μi2​. The sample mean Yˉ\bar{Y}Yˉ has mean μˉ=β0+β1Xˉ\bar{\mu} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \bar{X}μˉ​=β0​+β1​Xˉ and variance σ2/n\sigma^2/nσ2/n, so E{nYˉ2}=n(σ2/n+μˉ2)=σ2+nμˉ2E\{n\bar{Y}^2\} = n(\sigma^2/n + \bar{\mu}^2) = \sigma^2 + n\bar{\mu}^2E{nYˉ2}=n(σ2/n+μˉ​2)=σ2+nμˉ​2. Subtracting,

E{Syy}=nσ2+∑μi2−σ2−nμˉ2=(n−1)σ2+(∑μi2−nμˉ2).E\{S_{yy}\} = n\sigma^2 + \sum \mu_i^2 - \sigma^2 - n\bar{\mu}^2 = (n-1)\sigma^2 + \left(\sum \mu_i^2 - n\bar{\mu}^2\right).E{Syy​}=nσ2+∑μi2​−σ2−nμˉ​2=(n−1)σ2+(∑μi2​−nμˉ​2).

The final bracket is ∑(μi−μˉ)2=∑(β1(Xi−Xˉ))2=β12Sxx\sum (\mu_i - \bar{\mu})^2 = \sum \big(\beta_1 (X_i - \bar{X})\big)^2 = \beta_1^2 S_{xx}∑(μi​−μˉ​)2=∑(β1​(Xi​−Xˉ))2=β12​Sxx​. So E{Syy}=(n−1)σ2+β12SxxE\{S_{yy}\} = (n-1)\sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}E{Syy​}=(n−1)σ2+β12​Sxx​.

Combine. Subtracting the slope piece from the total piece,

E{SSE}=E{Syy}−E{b12Sxx}=[(n−1)σ2+β12Sxx]−[σ2+β12Sxx]=(n−2)σ2.E\{\mathrm{SSE}\} = E\{S_{yy}\} - E\{b_1^2 S_{xx}\} = \big[(n-1)\sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\big] - \big[\sigma^2 + \beta_1^2 S_{xx}\big] = (n-2)\sigma^2 .E{SSE}=E{Syy​}−E{b12​Sxx​}=[(n−1)σ2+β12​Sxx​]−[σ2+β12​Sxx​]=(n−2)σ2.

Therefore E{MSE}=E{SSE}/(n−2)=σ2E\{\mathrm{MSE}\} = E\{\mathrm{SSE}\}/(n-2) = \sigma^2E{MSE}=E{SSE}/(n−2)=σ2: the divisor n−2n-2n−2 is exactly what makes MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE an unbiased estimator of σ2\sigma^2σ2. ■\blacksquare■

R and Python¶

Example 2.4: The estimated error spread for Toluca

Question. How much do work hours vary around the fitted line, in hours?

Intuition. Sum the squared residuals to get SSE, divide by n−2=23n-2 = 23n−2=23 to get MSE, and take the square root for sss, the typical size of a residual in hours.

Formula. SSE=∑ei2\mathrm{SSE} = \sum e_i^2SSE=∑ei2​, MSE=SSE/(n−2)\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)MSE=SSE/(n−2), s=MSEs = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}}s=MSE​.

Computation.

n <- nrow(toluca)
SSE <- sum(e^2)
MSE <- SSE / (n - 2)
s <- sqrt(MSE)
round(c(n = n, SSE = SSE, MSE = MSE, s = s), 2)
       n      SSE      MSE        s
   25.00 54825.46  2383.72    48.82
n = len(toluca)
SSE = np.sum(e ** 2)
MSE = SSE / (n - 2)
s = np.sqrt(MSE)
print(n, round(SSE, 2), round(MSE, 2), round(s, 2))
25 54825.46 2383.72 48.82

Interpretation. The error sum of squares is SSE=54,825\mathrm{SSE} = 54{,}825SSE=54,825, giving MSE=2384\mathrm{MSE} = 2384MSE=2384 and s=48.8s = 48.8s=48.8 hours. So even knowing a run’s lot size, the model’s prediction of its hours is typically off by around 49 hours. Compared with a mean of about 312 hours, that is substantial run-to-run variability, and it is the raw material for every standard error in the next section.

Try it 2.4

Suppose a careless analyst divides SSE by n=25n = 25n=25 instead of n−2=23n - 2 = 23n−2=23. What value of s2s^2s2 would they report, and would it be too large or too small as an estimate of σ2\sigma^2σ2?

Solution

They would report 54,825/25=219354{,}825 / 25 = 219354,825/25=2193, smaller than the correct MSE=2384\mathrm{MSE} = 2384MSE=2384. Dividing by too large a number makes the estimate too small, so on average it understates σ2\sigma^2σ2: this is a biased (low) estimate. That value 2193 is exactly the maximum-likelihood estimate of σ2\sigma^2σ2 from 2.6 Maximum likelihood under normal errors, which is why the book uses n−2n-2n−2 for inference instead.

Theorem 2.8 says the divisor n−2n-2n−2 is the one that is right on average, and repeated sampling is the way to watch that claim settle.

What to notice. Individual values of MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE scatter widely, most of them landing anywhere from about 1200 to about 4000, yet their average walks steadily toward 2383.4. Try this. Press Draw 1000 twice and compare the two means: the n−2n-2n−2 divisor lands on σ2\sigma^2σ2 while the nnn divisor stays about 8 percent low no matter how many samples you add, which is what bias means. Back to Section 2.4.

2.5 Sampling behavior and the Gauss-Markov theorem¶

Intuition¶

The estimates b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ are computed from a particular sample of 25 runs. A different 25 runs, made under the same conditions, would give slightly different estimates. So b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ are themselves random: they have distributions, called sampling distributions, across the repeated samples we could have drawn. Figure 15 makes this concrete by simulating 60 fresh samples at the Toluca lot sizes and fitting each: the fitted lines scatter around the true mean line, and they fan out most where XXX is far from Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ.

Two questions organize this section. Are b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ correct on average (unbiased)? And how much do they vary from sample to sample (their variances)? The Gauss-Markov theorem then delivers a strong payoff: among all the sensible estimators one might invent, least squares has the smallest variance.

Formula¶

Both estimators are unbiased, and their variances are

E{b1}=β1,Var⁡{b1}=σ2Sxx;E{b0}=β0,Var⁡{b0}=σ2(1n+Xˉ2Sxx).E\{b_1\} = \beta_1, \quad \operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}; \qquad E\{b_0\} = \beta_0, \quad \operatorname{Var}\{b_0\} = \sigma^2\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right).E{b1​}=β1​,Var{b1​}=Sxx​σ2​;E{b0​}=β0​,Var{b0​}=σ2(n1​+Sxx​Xˉ2​).
Theorem 2.9: Means and variances of the least-squares estimators

Under the simple linear regression model, b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ are unbiased, with

E{b1}=β1,Var⁡{b1}=σ2Sxx;E{b0}=β0,Var⁡{b0}=σ2(1n+Xˉ2Sxx).E\{b_1\} = \beta_1, \quad \operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}}; \qquad E\{b_0\} = \beta_0, \quad \operatorname{Var}\{b_0\} = \sigma^2\left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right).E{b1​}=β1​,Var{b1​}=Sxx​σ2​;E{b0​}=β0​,Var{b0​}=σ2(n1​+Sxx​Xˉ2​).

  • Var⁡{b1}=σ2/Sxx\operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} = \sigma^2/S_{xx}Var{b1​}=σ2/Sxx​ shrinks when the errors are small (σ2\sigma^2σ2 low) or the predictor is spread wide (SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ large). Spreading your XXX values out buys precision.

  • Var⁡{b0}\operatorname{Var}\{b_0\}Var{b0​} carries an extra Xˉ2/Sxx\bar{X}^2/S_{xx}Xˉ2/Sxx​ term because the intercept lives far off at X=0X = 0X=0, and tilting the line pivots it there.

Figure 16 makes the first fact visible. When the lot sizes are bunched together, a little noise tips the slope wildly; when they are spread wide, the same noise barely moves it.

Replacing the unknown σ2\sigma^2σ2 by its estimate MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE gives the estimated variances s2{b1}=MSE/Sxxs^2\{b_1\} = \mathrm{MSE}/S_{xx}s2{b1​}=MSE/Sxx​ and s2{b0}=MSE(1/n+Xˉ2/Sxx)s^2\{b_0\} = \mathrm{MSE}\big(1/n + \bar{X}^2/S_{xx}\big)s2{b0​}=MSE(1/n+Xˉ2/Sxx​), whose square roots are the standard errors s{b1}s\{b_1\}s{b1​} and s{b0}s\{b_0\}s{b0​} that software prints.

Derivation (unbiasedness and variances)¶

Proof (mean and variance of b1b_1b1​). The key is to write b1b_1b1​ as a weighted sum of the responses. Since ∑(Xi−Xˉ)Yˉ=0\sum (X_i - \bar{X}) \bar{Y} = 0∑(Xi​−Xˉ)Yˉ=0,

b1=SxySxx=∑(Xi−Xˉ)(Yi−Yˉ)Sxx=∑i=1nkiYi,ki=Xi−XˉSxx.b_1 = \frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}} = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar{X})(Y_i - \bar{Y})}{S_{xx}} = \sum_{i=1}^n k_i Y_i, \qquad k_i = \frac{X_i - \bar{X}}{S_{xx}} .b1​=Sxx​Sxy​​=Sxx​∑(Xi​−Xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)​=i=1∑n​ki​Yi​,ki​=Sxx​Xi​−Xˉ​.

The weights kik_iki​ depend only on the fixed XXX values and satisfy three facts, each a one-line computation:

∑ki=∑(Xi−Xˉ)Sxx=0,∑kiXi=∑(Xi−Xˉ)XiSxx=SxxSxx=1,∑ki2=∑(Xi−Xˉ)2Sxx2=1Sxx.\sum k_i = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar X)}{S_{xx}} = 0, \qquad \sum k_i X_i = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar X)X_i}{S_{xx}} = \frac{S_{xx}}{S_{xx}} = 1, \qquad \sum k_i^2 = \frac{\sum (X_i - \bar X)^2}{S_{xx}^2} = \frac{1}{S_{xx}} .∑ki​=Sxx​∑(Xi​−Xˉ)​=0,∑ki​Xi​=Sxx​∑(Xi​−Xˉ)Xi​​=Sxx​Sxx​​=1,∑ki2​=Sxx2​∑(Xi​−Xˉ)2​=Sxx​1​.

Unbiasedness. Using E{Yi}=β0+β1XiE\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_iE{Yi​}=β0​+β1​Xi​,

E{b1}=∑kiE{Yi}=β0∑ki+β1∑kiXi=β0(0)+β1(1)=β1.E\{b_1\} = \sum k_i E\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 \sum k_i + \beta_1 \sum k_i X_i = \beta_0 (0) + \beta_1 (1) = \beta_1 .E{b1​}=∑ki​E{Yi​}=β0​∑ki​+β1​∑ki​Xi​=β0​(0)+β1​(1)=β1​.

Variance. The YiY_iYi​ are uncorrelated with common variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, so variances of a weighted sum add with squared weights:

Var⁡{b1}=∑ki2Var⁡{Yi}=σ2∑ki2=σ2Sxx.■\operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} = \sum k_i^2 \operatorname{Var}\{Y_i\} = \sigma^2 \sum k_i^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{S_{xx}} . \qquad \blacksquareVar{b1​}=∑ki2​Var{Yi​}=σ2∑ki2​=Sxx​σ2​.■

Proof (mean and variance of b0b_0b0​). Write b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉ=∑miYib_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1 \bar{X} = \sum m_i Y_ib0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ=∑mi​Yi​ with mi=1n−Xˉkim_i = \tfrac{1}{n} - \bar{X} k_imi​=n1​−Xˉki​. Then ∑mi=1\sum m_i = 1∑mi​=1 and ∑miXi=Xˉ−Xˉ=0\sum m_i X_i = \bar X - \bar X = 0∑mi​Xi​=Xˉ−Xˉ=0, so E{b0}=β0∑mi+β1∑miXi=β0E\{b_0\} = \beta_0 \sum m_i + \beta_1 \sum m_i X_i = \beta_0E{b0​}=β0​∑mi​+β1​∑mi​Xi​=β0​. For the variance, using ∑ki=0\sum k_i = 0∑ki​=0 and ∑ki2=1/Sxx\sum k_i^2 = 1/S_{xx}∑ki2​=1/Sxx​,

Var⁡{b0}=σ2∑mi2=σ2∑(1n−Xˉki)2=σ2(1n−2Xˉn∑ki+Xˉ2∑ki2)=σ2(1n+Xˉ2Sxx).■\operatorname{Var}\{b_0\} = \sigma^2 \sum m_i^2 = \sigma^2 \sum \left(\frac{1}{n} - \bar{X} k_i\right)^2 = \sigma^2 \left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{2\bar X}{n}\sum k_i + \bar{X}^2 \sum k_i^2\right) = \sigma^2 \left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{\bar{X}^2}{S_{xx}}\right). \qquad \blacksquareVar{b0​}=σ2∑mi2​=σ2∑(n1​−Xˉki​)2=σ2(n1​−n2Xˉ​∑ki​+Xˉ2∑ki2​)=σ2(n1​+Sxx​Xˉ2​).■

Derivation (Gauss-Markov: b1b_1b1​ is BLUE)¶

Theorem 2.10: Gauss-Markov theorem (simple linear regression)

Under the simple linear regression model (linear mean, constant variance, uncorrelated errors, with no normality assumed), among all estimators of β1\beta_1β1​ that are linear in the YiY_iYi​ and unbiased, the least-squares estimator b1b_1b1​ has the smallest variance; the same holds for b0b_0b0​. We say b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ are the best linear unbiased estimators (BLUE).

Proof. Consider any linear estimator β^1∗=∑ciYi\hat\beta_1^{\ast} = \sum c_i Y_iβ^​1∗​=∑ci​Yi​ with fixed weights cic_ici​. Its expectation is ∑ci(β0+β1Xi)=β0∑ci+β1∑ciXi\sum c_i(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i) = \beta_0 \sum c_i + \beta_1 \sum c_i X_i∑ci​(β0​+β1​Xi​)=β0​∑ci​+β1​∑ci​Xi​. For this to equal β1\beta_1β1​ for every possible β0\beta_0β0​ and β1\beta_1β1​, the weights must satisfy

∑ci=0and∑ciXi=1.\sum c_i = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum c_i X_i = 1 .∑ci​=0and∑ci​Xi​=1.

Write ci=ki+dic_i = k_i + d_ici​=ki​+di​, splitting each weight into the least-squares weight kik_iki​ and a deviation did_idi​. Because both cic_ici​ and kik_iki​ satisfy the two unbiasedness constraints, the deviations satisfy ∑di=0\sum d_i = 0∑di​=0 and ∑diXi=0\sum d_i X_i = 0∑di​Xi​=0. Now the cross term drops out:

∑kidi=∑Xi−XˉSxxdi=1Sxx(∑Xidi−Xˉ∑di)=1Sxx(0−0)=0.\sum k_i d_i = \sum \frac{X_i - \bar X}{S_{xx}} d_i = \frac{1}{S_{xx}}\left(\sum X_i d_i - \bar X \sum d_i\right) = \frac{1}{S_{xx}}(0 - 0) = 0 .∑ki​di​=∑Sxx​Xi​−Xˉ​di​=Sxx​1​(∑Xi​di​−Xˉ∑di​)=Sxx​1​(0−0)=0.

Therefore

Var⁡{β^1∗}=σ2∑ci2=σ2∑(ki+di)2=σ2∑ki2+σ2∑di2=Var⁡{b1}+σ2∑di2.\operatorname{Var}\{\hat\beta_1^{\ast}\} = \sigma^2 \sum c_i^2 = \sigma^2 \sum (k_i + d_i)^2 = \sigma^2 \sum k_i^2 + \sigma^2 \sum d_i^2 = \operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} + \sigma^2 \sum d_i^2 .Var{β^​1∗​}=σ2∑ci2​=σ2∑(ki​+di​)2=σ2∑ki2​+σ2∑di2​=Var{b1​}+σ2∑di2​.

Since σ2∑di2≥0\sigma^2 \sum d_i^2 \ge 0σ2∑di2​≥0, every linear unbiased competitor has variance at least that of b1b_1b1​, with equality only when all di=0d_i = 0di​=0, that is when the competitor is b1b_1b1​. The least-squares slope is BLUE. The same argument with weights mim_imi​ shows b0b_0b0​ is BLUE. ■\blacksquare■

Key idea

The Gauss-Markov theorem buys optimality cheaply. It uses only that the errors have mean zero, a common variance, and no correlation; it never assumes a normal distribution. So before any distributional model is in play, least squares is already the best you can do among linear unbiased estimators.

R and Python¶

Example 2.5: Standard errors of the Toluca coefficients

Question. How precisely are the intercept and slope pinned down by these 25 runs?

Intuition. Plug MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE, SxxS_{xx}Sxx​, nnn, and Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ into the estimated-variance formulas and take square roots to get standard errors, in the coefficients’ own units.

Formula. s{b1}=MSE/Sxxs\{b_1\} = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}/S_{xx}}s{b1​}=MSE/Sxx​​ and s{b0}=MSE (1/n+Xˉ2/Sxx)s\{b_0\} = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}\,(1/n + \bar{X}^2/S_{xx})}s{b0​}=MSE(1/n+Xˉ2/Sxx​)​.

Computation.

var_b1 <- MSE / Sxx
var_b0 <- MSE * (1 / n + mean(x)^2 / Sxx)
round(c(se_b0 = sqrt(var_b0), se_b1 = sqrt(var_b1)), 4)
  se_b0   se_b1
26.1774  0.3470
var_b1 = MSE / Sxx
var_b0 = MSE * (1 / n + x.mean() ** 2 / Sxx)
print(round(np.sqrt(var_b0), 4), round(np.sqrt(var_b1), 4))
26.1774 0.347

These are the same standard errors the built-in summary prints, alongside much more we will decode in Chapter 3.

Interpretation. The slope’s standard error is s{b1}=0.347s\{b_1\} = 0.347s{b1​}=0.347 hours per unit: the estimate 3.57 is known to well within an hour-per-unit, which is why the summary flags it as clearly nonzero. The intercept’s standard error is 26.18, much larger, which is nothing surprising: the intercept sits far from the data at X=0X = 0X=0, so it is estimated loosely. Both match the hand computation exactly and match summary and fit.summary().

The variance formulas are not just algebra; they describe the fanning bundle of lines in Figure 15. We can confirm both the unbiasedness and the slope-variance formula by simulation, drawing 5000 samples from the estimated model and refitting each. Figure 17 shows the histogram of the 5000 slope estimates.

set.seed(4210)
beta0 <- 62.366; beta1 <- 3.5702; sigma <- 48.82
xfix <- toluca$lotsize
Sxx_fix <- sum((xfix - mean(xfix))^2)
b1_sim <- replicate(5000, {
  ysim <- beta0 + beta1 * xfix + rnorm(length(xfix), 0, sigma)
  coef(lm(ysim ~ xfix))[["xfix"]]
})
round(c(mean_of_b1_hats = mean(b1_sim),
        true_beta1 = beta1,
        sd_of_b1_hats = sd(b1_sim),
        formula_se = sqrt(sigma^2 / Sxx_fix)), 4)
mean_of_b1_hats      true_beta1   sd_of_b1_hats      formula_se
         3.5699          3.5702          0.3479          0.3469
rng = np.random.default_rng(4210)
beta0, beta1, sigma = 62.366, 3.5702, 48.82
xfix = toluca["lotsize"].to_numpy()
Sxx_fix = np.sum((xfix - xfix.mean()) ** 2)
b1_hats = np.empty(5000)
for i in range(5000):
    ysim = beta0 + beta1 * xfix + rng.normal(0, sigma, size=xfix.size)
    b1_hats[i] = np.polyfit(xfix, ysim, 1)[0]
print(round(b1_hats.mean(), 4), beta1,
      round(b1_hats.std(ddof=1), 4),
      round(np.sqrt(sigma ** 2 / Sxx_fix), 4))
3.5675 3.5702 0.352 0.3469

The average of the 5000 slope estimates sits right on β1=3.5702\beta_1 = 3.5702β1​=3.5702 (unbiasedness), and their simulated standard deviation, 0.348 in R and 0.352 in Python, matches the formula value σ/Sxx=0.347\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}} = 0.347σ/Sxx​​=0.347. The two languages differ only in the last digit because they use different random number generators; the agreement with theory is the point.

Durable skill: Check a formula by simulating it

When a derivation hands you a formula for a mean or a variance, you can test it without more algebra: generate many datasets from a known model, compute the estimate on each, and compare the pile of estimates to what the formula predicted. If the simulated average and spread match, your derivation and your code probably agree. This habit, letting a random experiment audit a theoretical claim, transfers to every quantitative field and is exactly how you will sanity-check your own analyses long after this course.

Try it 2.5

For the Toluca fit, Sxx=19,800S_{xx} = 19{,}800Sxx​=19,800 and MSE=2384\mathrm{MSE} = 2384MSE=2384. Use the variance formula to compute s2{b1}s^2\{b_1\}s2{b1​} by hand, then explain in one sentence why spreading the lot sizes out more (increasing SxxS_{xx}Sxx​) would shrink s2{b1}s^2\{b_1\}s2{b1​}.

Solution

s2{b1}=MSE/Sxx=2384/19,800=0.1204s^2\{b_1\} = \mathrm{MSE}/S_{xx} = 2384/19{,}800 = 0.1204s2{b1​}=MSE/Sxx​=2384/19,800=0.1204, so s{b1}=0.1204=0.347s\{b_1\} = \sqrt{0.1204} = 0.347s{b1​}=0.1204​=0.347, matching Example 2.5. Because SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ sits in the denominator of Var⁡{b1}=σ2/Sxx\operatorname{Var}\{b_1\} = \sigma^2/S_{xx}Var{b1​}=σ2/Sxx​, a larger SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ divides σ2\sigma^2σ2 into a smaller number: doubling SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ would cut s2{b1}s^2\{b_1\}s2{b1​} exactly in half. Spreading the predictor values farther apart pins the slope down more tightly, for the same error variance σ2\sigma^2σ2.

The bundle of fitted lines in Figure 15 is easier to believe when you build it one sample at a time.

What to notice. Draw samples one at a time and no single b1b_1b1​ equals 3.5702, yet the pile they build is centered there. Try this. Press Draw 1000 and compare the SD of b1b_1b1​ readout with σ/Sxx=0.3469\sigma/\sqrt{S_{xx}} = 0.3469σ/Sxx​​=0.3469 sitting beside it: the variance formula of Theorem 2.9 is not an approximation, it is the width of this pile. Back to Section 2.5.

2.6 Maximum likelihood under normal errors¶

Intuition¶

So far we chose least squares because squared error is a reasonable penalty, and Gauss-Markov rewarded that choice with the best-linear-unbiased property, all without assuming any shape for the error distribution. Now suppose we add one assumption: the errors are normally distributed. A different principle, maximum likelihood, asks which parameter values make the data we actually observed most probable. Remarkably, under normal errors that principle points at the very same line. Figure 19 shows the two criteria, sum of squared errors and negative log-likelihood, bottoming out at exactly the same slope.

Formula¶

The normal error regression model (Definition 2.11) keeps everything from 2.1 The simple linear regression model and adds a shape:

Yi=β0+β1Xi+εi,εi∼iidN(0,σ2).Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2) .Yi​=β0​+β1​Xi​+εi​,εi​∼iidN(0,σ2).
Definition 2.11: Normal error regression model

The normal error regression model is the simple linear regression model with the added assumption that the errors are independent and normally distributed: Yi=β0+β1Xi+εiY_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​Xi​+εi​ with εi∼iidN(0,σ2)\varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, \sigma^2)εi​∼iidN(0,σ2).

Under normality the uncorrelated errors are now fully independent. The likelihood is the joint density of the observed YiY_iYi​ read as a function of the parameters:

L(β0,β1,σ2)=∏i=1n12πσ2exp⁡ ⁣(−(Yi−β0−β1Xi)22σ2).L(\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) .L(β0​,β1​,σ2)=i=1∏n​2πσ2​1​exp(−2σ2(Yi​−β0​−β1​Xi​)2​).

  • LLL is large for parameter values that make the observed data look typical, small for values that make it look freakish.

  • Maximum likelihood estimates are the β0,β1,σ2\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma^2β0​,β1​,σ2 that maximize LLL.

Derivation (maximum likelihood equals least squares)¶

Theorem 2.12: Maximum likelihood under normal errors

Under the normal error regression model, the maximum-likelihood estimates of the coefficients equal the least-squares estimates, β^0MLE=b0\hat\beta_0^{\text{MLE}} = b_0β^​0MLE​=b0​ and β^1MLE=b1\hat\beta_1^{\text{MLE}} = b_1β^​1MLE​=b1​, while the maximum-likelihood estimate of the variance is σ^MLE2=SSE/n\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}} = \mathrm{SSE}/nσ^MLE2​=SSE/n (biased low).

Proof. Maximizing LLL is easier through its logarithm, which is maximized at the same place because log⁡\loglog is increasing:

ln⁡L=−n2ln⁡(2π)−n2ln⁡σ2−12σ2∑i=1n(Yi−β0−β1Xi)2.\ln L = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\ln \sigma^2 - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2 .lnL=−2n​ln(2π)−2n​lnσ2−2σ21​i=1∑n​(Yi​−β0​−β1​Xi​)2.

Coefficients. Fix any σ2>0\sigma^2 > 0σ2>0. The first two terms do not involve β0\beta_0β0​ or β1\beta_1β1​, and the last term has −1/(2σ2)<0-1/(2\sigma^2) < 0−1/(2σ2)<0 multiplying ∑(Yi−β0−β1Xi)2\sum (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2∑(Yi​−β0​−β1​Xi​)2. Maximizing ln⁡L\ln LlnL over β0,β1\beta_0, \beta_1β0​,β1​ therefore means minimizing that sum of squares, which is exactly the least-squares criterion QQQ from 2.2 Least squares from first principles. So the maximum-likelihood estimates of the coefficients are the least-squares estimates:

β^0MLE=b0,β^1MLE=b1.\hat\beta_0^{\text{MLE}} = b_0, \qquad \hat\beta_1^{\text{MLE}} = b_1 .β^​0MLE​=b0​,β^​1MLE​=b1​.

Variance. Substitute b0,b1b_0, b_1b0​,b1​ so the sum of squares becomes SSE\mathrm{SSE}SSE, then differentiate ln⁡L\ln LlnL with respect to σ2\sigma^2σ2 and set it to zero:

∂ln⁡L∂σ2=−n2σ2+SSE2σ4=0⟹σ^MLE2=SSEn.\frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \sigma^2} = -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{2\sigma^4} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}} = \frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n} .∂σ2∂lnL​=−2σ2n​+2σ4SSE​=0⟹σ^MLE2​=nSSE​.

The maximum-likelihood variance estimate divides by nnn, not n−2n-2n−2. From 2.4 Estimating the error variance we know the nnn divisor is biased low, understating σ2\sigma^2σ2, because it ignores the two degrees of freedom spent on b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​. That is why the book, and all the inference in Chapter 3, uses the unbiased MSE=SSE/(n−2)\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)MSE=SSE/(n−2) rather than the maximum-likelihood σ^MLE2\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}σ^MLE2​. ■\blacksquare■

Key idea

Least squares and maximum likelihood are the same line seen through two lenses. Squared-error loss and the normal log-likelihood are optimized at the identical coefficients, so a choice made for algebraic convenience turns out to be the most-probable-data choice once the errors are normal.

R and Python¶

Example 2.6: The two variance estimates for Toluca

Question. How far apart are the unbiased MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE and the maximum-likelihood σ^MLE2\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}}σ^MLE2​ for these data?

Intuition. Both use the same SSE\mathrm{SSE}SSE; they differ only in the divisor, n−2=23n-2 = 23n−2=23 versus n=25n = 25n=25.

Formula. MSE=SSE/(n−2)\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)MSE=SSE/(n−2) and σ^MLE2=SSE/n\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}} = \mathrm{SSE}/nσ^MLE2​=SSE/n.

Computation.

sigma2_mle <- SSE / n
round(c(MSE_divisor_n_minus_2 = MSE, MLE_divisor_n = sigma2_mle), 2)
MSE_divisor_n_minus_2         MLE_divisor_n
              2383.72               2193.02
sigma2_mle = SSE / n
print(round(MSE, 2), round(sigma2_mle, 2))
2383.72 2193.02

Interpretation. The two estimates are 2384 (unbiased) and 2193 (maximum likelihood). The maximum-likelihood value is about 8% smaller, the size of the nnn versus n−2n-2n−2 correction at n=25n = 25n=25. For a large sample the gap would be negligible; for a small one it matters, and the course uses the unbiased MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE so that the standard errors and intervals in Chapter 3 are honest.

Try it 2.6

Explain in one or two sentences why maximizing the normal likelihood forces you to minimize the sum of squared errors, pointing to the specific piece of ln⁡L\ln LlnL that carries the coefficients.

Solution

In ln⁡L\ln LlnL the only term containing β0\beta_0β0​ and β1\beta_1β1​ is −12σ2∑(Yi−β0−β1Xi)2-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum (Y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 X_i)^2−2σ21​∑(Yi​−β0​−β1​Xi​)2. Its coefficient −1/(2σ2)-1/(2\sigma^2)−1/(2σ2) is negative, so making ln⁡L\ln LlnL as large as possible means making the sum of squares as small as possible. Maximizing the likelihood in the coefficients is minimizing SSE, the least-squares problem.

2.7 Chapter summary¶

This chapter built a simple linear regression from the ground up and proved the properties that make it trustworthy. Starting from the model Yi=β0+β1Xi+εiY_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​Xi​+εi​ and its three error assumptions, we defined the least-squares criterion and derived the estimators two independent ways, by calculus through the normal equations and by an algebraic identity that shows no other line has a smaller SSE. The residuals obey exact identities that double as a correctness check; the error variance is estimated by MSE=SSE/(n−2)\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)MSE=SSE/(n−2), whose n−2n-2n−2 divisor is exactly what makes it unbiased. Treating b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ as random over repeated samples gave their means and variances, the Gauss-Markov theorem showed they are best among linear unbiased estimators with no normality needed, and maximum likelihood under normal errors reproduced the very same line.

Key terms

You should now be able to

  • State the simple linear regression model and explain the job each error assumption does.

  • Derive the least-squares estimators two ways, by calculus and by the algebraic identity.

  • Compute b0b_0b0​, b1b_1b1​, fitted values, and residuals by hand and with software.

  • Prove the residual identities and use them as a built-in check on a fit.

  • Explain the n−2n-2n−2 divisor by deriving E{MSE}=σ2E\{\mathrm{MSE}\} = \sigma^2E{MSE}=σ2, and compute MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE and sss.

  • Derive the means and variances of b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ and prove that b1b_1b1​ is the best linear unbiased estimator.

  • Show that maximum likelihood under normal errors reproduces the least-squares estimates.

Where this fits. This chapter is the first full trip around the workflow of The modeling workflow. It carried the Toluca question through ASK and EXPLORE, settled into FIT, and took first steps into CHECK (the residual identities and the residual plot) and USE (reading the slope in hours per unit). Chapter 1 argued that regression is a way of thinking about how one quantity moves with another; this chapter turned that idea into a specific, computable line and proved the properties that make it trustworthy. Everything here is point estimation: single best guesses for β0\beta_0β0​, β1\beta_1β1​, and σ2\sigma^2σ2. What we have not yet done is quantify uncertainty with intervals and tests. That is Chapter 3, which takes the sampling distributions sketched here, adds the normal error assumption in full, and builds ttt intervals for the slope and intercept, the ANOVA decomposition (3.6 The analysis of variance approach), the FFF test (3.7 The F test and its equivalence to the t test), and the difference between a confidence interval for a mean response and a prediction interval for a new run (3.5 Prediction interval for a new observation). The exact Toluca fit set here (b1=3.5702b_1 = 3.5702b1​=3.5702, MSE=2384\mathrm{MSE} = 2384MSE=2384) carries forward unchanged, now with inference attached. It travels further still: Chapter 5 reruns the same slope through a permutation test (5.2 The permutation test for the slope) and checks its p-value against Chapter 3’s, and in Chapter 7 the same estimators reappear in matrix form (7.1 The model and least squares in matrix form), where the two-line normal equations become a single equation X′Xb=X′Y\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y}X′Xb=X′Y and the Gauss-Markov proof (7.6 The Gauss-Markov theorem) generalizes to any number of predictors at once.

2.8 Frequently asked questions¶

Q1. Why square the residuals instead of taking absolute values? Both are reasonable losses. Squaring makes the objective smooth and differentiable, so calculus gives a clean closed-form solution (the normal equations), and it is exactly the loss for which the Gauss-Markov and normal-likelihood results hold. Absolute-value loss gives “least absolute deviations” regression, which is more resistant to outliers but has no simple formula and needs iterative solving. The course starts with squared error because it is where the theory is cleanest.

Q2. Is the intercept b0=62.37b_0 = 62.37b0​=62.37 really “hours to produce zero units”? No, not meaningfully. A lot size of zero is far outside the data (the smallest run was 20 units), so the intercept is an extrapolation. Read it as the number that anchors the line’s height, computed so the line passes through (Xˉ,Yˉ)(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})(Xˉ,Yˉ), not as a physical setup time. Interpreting an intercept literally only makes sense when X=0X = 0X=0 is inside or near the observed range.

Q3. What is the difference between an error εi\varepsilon_iεi​ and a residual eie_iei​? The error εi=Yi−(β0+β1Xi)\varepsilon_i = Y_i - (\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i)εi​=Yi​−(β0​+β1​Xi​) is the gap to the true, unknown line, and we can never observe it. The residual ei=Yi−Y^ie_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_iei​=Yi​−Y^i​ is the gap to our estimated line, and we compute it directly. Residuals are our visible estimates of the invisible errors, which is why we estimate σ2\sigma^2σ2 from them.

Q4. Why divide SSE by n−2n-2n−2 and not n−1n-1n−1 like an ordinary sample variance? A sample variance divides by n−1n-1n−1 because it estimates one quantity, the mean, from the data. Regression estimates two, the intercept and slope, before measuring residuals, so it spends two degrees of freedom, leaving n−2n-2n−2. The derivation in 2.4 Estimating the error variance shows E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2E\{\mathrm{SSE}\} = (n-2)\sigma^2E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2 exactly, so n−2n-2n−2 is the divisor that makes MSE\mathrm{MSE}MSE unbiased.

Q5. Do I need the errors to be normal for least squares to work? No. The least-squares estimates, their unbiasedness, their variance formulas, and the Gauss-Markov optimality all hold with no assumption about the error distribution’s shape, only mean zero, constant variance, and uncorrelated errors. Normality is an extra assumption, added in 2.6 Maximum likelihood under normal errors and used in Chapter 3 to build exact ttt and FFF intervals and tests.

Q6. Why does the bundle of fitted lines in Figure 15 pinch in the middle? Every least-squares line passes through (Xˉ,Yˉ)(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})(Xˉ,Yˉ) (residual property 5), so near Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ the lines can only wobble a little. Away from Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ, a small change in the slope pivots the line a large vertical distance, so the lines fan out. The variance of a fitted value grows with distance from Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ, which Chapter 3 turns into the curved shape of a confidence band.

Q7. R prints 4.45e-10 and Python prints 4.45e-10 for the slope’s p-value, but we did not assume normality. Where did that come from? Those p-values and the standard errors’ t-values do use the normal error model, and we will justify them properly in Chapter 3. This chapter shows the standard errors themselves, which come from the variance formulas and need no normality; the significance stars and p-values are a preview of the inference to come.

2.10 Exam practice¶

The problems below are written in the style of this course’s exams: each asks you to explain in full sentences, not just to produce a number. On the real exam a bare answer earns little credit, and correct reasoning with a small slip earns most of it, so practice writing the reasoning out. Work each one on paper before opening its model answer. Where output is shown, it is genuine software output from toluca.csv.

EP 2.1. Explain why the line describes the mean, not the response. A first-time reader says “the model claims work hours are a straight-line function of lot size.” Explain why that is not what the simple linear regression model claims, and state precisely which quantity the straight line does describe. Then explain what job the constant-variance assumption Var⁡{εi}=σ2\operatorname{Var}\{\varepsilon_i\} = \sigma^2Var{εi​}=σ2 does that the mean-line equation alone does not.

Model answer

The model equation is Yi=β0+β1Xi+εiY_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​Xi​+εi​, so each observed hours value is a straight-line piece plus a random error. What lies exactly on the line is therefore not YiY_iYi​ itself but its mean, E{Yi}=β0+β1XiE\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_iE{Yi​}=β0​+β1​Xi​. Any single run sits above or below the line by its error εi\varepsilon_iεi​, which is exactly why two lots of the same size took different amounts of time. The mean-line equation fixes only where the center of the response sits at each lot size; it says nothing about how tightly the runs cluster around that center. The constant-variance assumption supplies that missing piece: it says the runs scatter by the same amount σ2\sigma^2σ2 at every lot size, so the band around the line keeps a constant width. Without it the line could be right on average yet much more trustworthy at some lot sizes than at others, and every standard error later in the chapter would need a different formula.

A weak answer says “YYY is linear in XXX” and forgets the error term, or names the constant-variance assumption without saying that its job is to hold the width of the scatter equal across all XXX.

EP 2.2. A student claims least squares cannot be beaten. A student writes: “The Gauss-Markov theorem proves that b1b_1b1​ has the smallest variance of any estimator of β1\beta_1β1​, so it is impossible to estimate the slope more precisely than least squares does.” Evaluate this claim. Where it overreaches, state exactly what the theorem does and does not promise.

Model answer

The claim overreaches. Gauss-Markov says b1b_1b1​ is best only inside a specific class: estimators that are linear in the responses YiY_iYi​ and unbiased for β1\beta_1β1​. Among that class its variance σ2/Sxx\sigma^2/S_{xx}σ2/Sxx​ is the smallest, and that is the whole of the promise. The theorem does not say b1b_1b1​ beats every conceivable estimator. A biased estimator, such as a shrinkage (ridge) slope, can have a smaller variance and even a smaller mean squared error than b1b_1b1​, buying that at the price of a little bias; nonlinear estimators sit outside the theorem’s scope entirely. The result also rests on its hypotheses of mean-zero, constant-variance, uncorrelated errors. If the errors have unequal variances or are correlated, ordinary least squares need not be best, and a weighted or generalized least-squares estimator can do better. So the precise reading is: no linear unbiased estimator beats b1b_1b1​ under the stated error conditions. That is a real and useful optimality, not the universal one the student stated.

A weak answer accepts “smallest variance of any estimator” without restricting to linear and unbiased estimators, or forgets that the constant-variance and uncorrelated-error hypotheses are what the guarantee depends on.

EP 2.3. Interpret the reverse regression in context. An analyst reverses the chapter’s fit and regresses lot size on work hours, reusing toluca.csv. The genuine R and Python output is below.

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) -1.85825    7.41053  -0.251    0.804
hours        0.23011    0.02236  10.290 4.45e-10 ***
---
Residual standard error: 12.4 on 23 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.8215,	Adjusted R-squared:  0.8138
                 coef    std err          t      P>|t|      [0.025      0.975]
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Intercept     -1.8583      7.411     -0.251      0.804     -17.188      13.472
hours          0.2301      0.022     10.290      0.000       0.184       0.276

(a) Interpret the reverse slope 0.2301 in the units of this problem. (b) The forward fit (hours on lot size) had slope 3.5702, whose reciprocal is 1/3.5702=0.2801/3.5702 = 0.2801/3.5702=0.280. Explain why the reverse slope 0.2301 is not that reciprocal. (c) Both directions report the same R2=0.8215R^2 = 0.8215R2=0.8215. Explain why that agreement is expected, and say what the product of the two slopes equals.

Model answer

(a) The reverse slope says that two runs differing by one work hour differ, on average, by about 0.23 units of lot size, in units of lot-size units per hour, over the observed range. It is a description of how lot size tracks hours, not a causal or physical rate.

(b) Regressing YYY on XXX minimizes the vertical gaps (errors in hours), while regressing XXX on YYY minimizes the horizontal gaps (errors in lot size). These are different minimizations answering different questions, so their slopes are not reciprocals. Algebraically the forward slope is Sxy/Sxx=3.5702S_{xy}/S_{xx} = 3.5702Sxy​/Sxx​=3.5702 and the reverse slope is Sxy/Syy=0.2301S_{xy}/S_{yy} = 0.2301Sxy​/Syy​=0.2301. The reciprocal 0.280 would be the reverse slope only if the fit were perfect (R2=1R^2 = 1R2=1). Because the fit is imperfect here, the reverse slope 0.2301 comes out smaller than 0.280.

(c) R2R^2R2 is the squared correlation between the two variables, a symmetric quantity that does not care which variable is called the response, so both directions must report the same value 0.8215. The product of the two slopes is SxySxx⋅SxySyy=Sxy2SxxSyy=R2=0.8215\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\cdot\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{yy}} = \frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}} = R^2 = 0.8215Sxx​Sxy​​⋅Syy​Sxy​​=Sxx​Syy​Sxy2​​=R2=0.8215, which also shows why they are reciprocals (product=1\text{product} = 1product=1) only when R2=1R^2 = 1R2=1.

A weak answer reads the reverse slope as “3.57 backwards” and expects the reciprocal, or cannot say why the two slopes multiply to R2R^2R2 rather than to 1.

EP 2.4. What would change if the lot sizes were bunched? The engineers happened to record lot sizes spread from 20 to 120 units, giving Sxx=19,800S_{xx} = 19{,}800Sxx​=19,800. Suppose instead every run had been scheduled between 60 and 80 units, so the same 25 runs carried a much smaller SxxS_{xx}Sxx​, about 3,0003{,}0003,000, with the true line and σ2\sigma^2σ2 unchanged. Explain the direction of the change, and the reason, for (a) the slope’s standard error, (b) the spread of the bundle of plausible fitted lines, and (c) your ability to interpret the intercept b0b_0b0​. Then say what would not change.

Model answer

(a) The slope standard error s{b1}=MSE/Sxxs\{b_1\} = \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}/S_{xx}}s{b1​}=MSE/Sxx​​ would grow. Dropping SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ from 19,80019{,}80019,800 to about 3,0003{,}0003,000 shrinks the denominator by a factor of roughly 6.6, so the variance σ2/Sxx\sigma^2/S_{xx}σ2/Sxx​ rises by that factor and the standard error by its square root, about 2.6 times. Same data effort, a far noisier slope, because bunched predictors give the line little horizontal purchase.

(b) The bundle of fitted lines from repeated samples would fan out much more. When the XXX values sit close together, a small amount of error tips a line steeply, so the slope is pinned down loosely, exactly the narrow-spread panel in Figure 16.

(c) Interpreting b0b_0b0​ as anything physical would be even less defensible. The intercept is the fitted height at X=0X = 0X=0, and with lot sizes now confined to 60 to 80, zero is farther outside the data than before, so the intercept is a more extreme extrapolation. Its own standard error, which carries the term Xˉ2/Sxx\bar{X}^2/S_{xx}Xˉ2/Sxx​, would also balloon as SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ falls.

What would not change: the estimators stay unbiased, since E{b1}=β1E\{b_1\} = \beta_1E{b1​}=β1​ regardless of the predictor spread, and σ2\sigma^2σ2 and the true line are the same. On average the slope is still correct; it is just much less precise.

A weak answer says precision “gets worse” without tying it to SxxS_{xx}Sxx​ in the denominator, or wrongly claims the estimates become biased when the predictors are bunched.

EP 2.5. Two errors in a hand-fit argument. A classmate fits a line by hand, reports residuals that sum to exactly zero, and concludes: “Since ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0, my fit must be the least-squares line, and I can now estimate σ2\sigma^2σ2 by dividing SSE by nnn.” Identify the two separate errors in this reasoning, and give the correct statement in each case.

Model answer

First error: ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0 does not prove a least-squares fit. The condition is necessary but not sufficient. The first normal equation forces ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0 for the least-squares line with an intercept, so every least-squares fit has it; but so does any other line drawn through the point of means (Xˉ,Yˉ)(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})(Xˉ,Yˉ), including one with the wrong slope and a compensating intercept. The identity that actually singles out least squares is the second normal equation, ∑Xiei=0\sum X_i e_i = 0∑Xi​ei​=0. To confirm the fit is least squares the classmate must check that the residuals are orthogonal to the predictor as well, not merely that they balance to zero.

Second error: dividing SSE by nnn is biased. Two degrees of freedom were spent estimating b0b_0b0​ and b1b_1b1​ before the residuals were measured, so E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2E\{\mathrm{SSE}\} = (n-2)\sigma^2E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2, and only MSE=SSE/(n−2)\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)MSE=SSE/(n−2) is unbiased for σ2\sigma^2σ2. Dividing by nnn (the maximum-likelihood divisor) understates σ2\sigma^2σ2, most noticeably when nnn is small. The correct estimator is s2=SSE/(n−2)s^2 = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)s2=SSE/(n−2).

A weak answer treats ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0 as proof of least squares while ignoring ∑Xiei=0\sum X_i e_i = 0∑Xi​ei​=0, or defends the divisor nnn without recognizing that it is biased low.

Resumen del capítulo (en español)

Este capítulo presenta la regresión lineal simple (simple linear regression), el modelo Yi=β0+β1Xi+εiY_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_iYi​=β0​+β1​Xi​+εi​, usando los datos de la Toluca Company: horas de trabajo frente al tamaño del lote de producción en 25 corridas. El modelo separa cada observación en una parte sistemática, la recta media E{Y}=β0+β1XE\{Y\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 XE{Y}=β0​+β1​X, y un error (error) aleatorio con media cero, varianza constante σ2\sigma^2σ2 y sin correlación entre observaciones. Ninguna suposición sobre la forma de la distribución se necesita todavía.

El método de mínimos cuadrados (least squares) elige la recta que minimiza la suma de los cuadrados de las distancias verticales, Q=∑(Yi−b0−b1Xi)2Q = \sum (Y_i - b_0 - b_1 X_i)^2Q=∑(Yi​−b0​−b1​Xi​)2. Derivamos los estimadores de dos maneras: por cálculo, obteniendo las ecuaciones normales (normal equations) y las soluciones b1=Sxy/Sxxb_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}b1​=Sxy​/Sxx​ y b0=Yˉ−b1Xˉb_0 = \bar{Y} - b_1\bar{X}b0​=Yˉ−b1​Xˉ; y por una identidad algebraica que demuestra que ninguna otra recta tiene una SSE menor. Para la Toluca, b0=62.37b_0 = 62.37b0​=62.37 y b1=3.5702b_1 = 3.5702b1​=3.5702: cada unidad adicional en el lote agrega unas 3.57 horas.

Los residuos (residuals) ei=Yi−Y^ie_i = Y_i - \hat{Y}_iei​=Yi​−Y^i​ cumplen identidades exactas: suman cero, son ortogonales al predictor y a los valores ajustados, y la recta pasa por (Xˉ,Yˉ)(\bar{X}, \bar{Y})(Xˉ,Yˉ). La varianza del error σ2\sigma^2σ2 se estima con MSE=SSE/(n−2)\mathrm{MSE} = \mathrm{SSE}/(n-2)MSE=SSE/(n−2); el divisor n−2n-2n−2 hace que el estimador sea insesgado (unbiased), lo cual demostramos probando que E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2E\{\mathrm{SSE}\} = (n-2)\sigma^2E{SSE}=(n−2)σ2. Para la Toluca, SSE=54,825\mathrm{SSE} = 54{,}825SSE=54,825, MSE=2384\mathrm{MSE} = 2384MSE=2384 y s=48.8s = 48.8s=48.8 horas.

Finalmente estudiamos el comportamiento muestral de los estimadores: b0b_0b0​ y b1b_1b1​ son insesgados, con varianzas σ2/Sxx\sigma^2/S_{xx}σ2/Sxx​ y σ2(1/n+Xˉ2/Sxx)\sigma^2(1/n + \bar{X}^2/S_{xx})σ2(1/n+Xˉ2/Sxx​). El teorema de Gauss-Markov (Gauss-Markov theorem) demuestra que b1b_1b1​ es el mejor estimador lineal insesgado (de mínima varianza). Bajo errores normales, la máxima verosimilitud (maximum likelihood) produce exactamente los mismos estimadores de mínimos cuadrados, con σ^MLE2=SSE/n\hat\sigma^2_{\text{MLE}} = \mathrm{SSE}/nσ^MLE2​=SSE/n. El Capítulo 3 usará estas distribuciones muestrales para construir intervalos de confianza y pruebas de hipótesis.
